title: One more city, how many more routes?
hook: A computer is fast. Can it just try every order of 9 cities, or 19?

knows: that a trip visits places in some order
doesNotKnow: that the number of orders is a factorial
how fast the number of orders grows with each added city

misconception: Adding one more city adds a few more routes to check, so a computer just checks them all.
objective: The learner can explain that with home fixed, k cities can be visited in k × (k-1) × ... × 1 orders, so each added city multiplies the count (6, 24, 120 ... 362,880 for 9) and checking every order soon becomes impossible.

claims.text: Starting from a fixed home, 3 cities can be visited in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders and 4 cities in 24.
claims.source: Demo.tsx perms(k) lists every order and draws it; perms(3).length = 6, perms(4).length = 24 (builder ran in Node). Arithmetic: 3! = 6, 4! = 24.

claims.text: Visiting 9 other cities once each from a fixed home gives 9 × 8 × ... × 1 = 362,880 orders; counting home as a 10th free choice would give 3,628,800.
claims.source: Arithmetic: 9! = 362,880, 10! = 3,628,800 (builder computed with BigInt in Node). Demo.tsx fact().

claims.text: Adding city k multiplies the count by k, because the new city can go in k places in every old order.
claims.source: Insertion argument: an order of k-1 cities has k gaps (before the first, between, after the last), so k! = k × (k-1)!.

claims.text: With home plus 19 cities there are 121,645,100,408,832,000 orders: about 3.9 years at a billion checks a second.
Real route planners use cleverer methods than checking every order.
claims.source: Applegate, Bixby, Chvatal and Cook, The Traveling Salesman Problem: A Computational Study (2006): branch-and-cut (Concorde) solves instances with thousands of cities exactly; heuristics such as Lin-Kernighan give near-optimal tours. TSP is NP-hard (Karp 1972), so no method is known to be fast on every instance; the lesson does not claim one is.

recall.question: A delivery van already has 10 stops and you add an 11th. Roughly what happens to the number of possible stop orders?
recall.why: The new stop can go into any of 11 places in every existing order, so the number of orders is multiplied by 11 (10! becomes 11!).
